newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: New U.N. chief Annan touts staff cuts and money.
newsitem.headline: New U.N. chief Annan touts staff cuts and money.

text.p: Beginning work as the new U.N. secretary-general, Kofi Annan promised to streamline the bureaucracy of a world body in debt because the United States has refused to pay its bills.

The 58-year-old Ghanaian, a U.N. career official, began his first full day in office on Thursday, succeeding Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, whose bid for a second five-year term was blocked by Washington in a bitter campaign for allegedly not instituting enough U.N. reforms.
"The member states have made it clear that they want changes and they have given us unanimous support," Annan said.

"And I think together we can achieve a lot, bring about the reforms that are necessary, encourage the member states to work together, to honour their commitment to the organisation and together make the changes that are required if we are to make the United Nations as relevant as it ought to be as we move into the 21st century," he added.
His spokesman, Fred Eckhard, said Annan intended to press member states immediately on setting priorities.

"His first job is nailing down governments on some essential agreement on what the work of this organisation is to be. This means establishing priorities and then re-arranging the administration to do that job and adjusting the finances."

"Administrative processes must be streamlined for more efficiency and effectiveness," Eckhard said. "It is time now to make a decision and he would like that decision to be made in the early days of his administration."

Annan in December had asked for the resignations of 23 undersecretaries-general and assistant secretaries-general, which Eckhard said he had now received. Some, however, are expected to be reappointed.
He also appointed a "provisional" staff for his executive office led by Iqbal Riza of Pakistan, a former official in the peacekeeping department Annan had led for the past three years.

Greeted by an honour guard of U.N. police and cheering staff members, Annan later on Thursday kept with the tradition of his predecessors and visited the U.N. meditation room. His wife Nane, a Swedish artist and lawyer, accompanied him to the entrance of the room but did not go inside.
"This is my first day. It is like the first day in school. Everyone expects a lot from you and you get into it with considerable trepidation," Annan said.

U.N. officials said he had spoken to President Bill Clinton shortly after being sworn in by the U.N. General Assembly on Dec. 17 and was invited to come to Washington as soon as a date could be arranged, possibly this month.

Annan already has an invitation from Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, to discuss his plans before the committee in an effort to break the funding logjam, on which the success of his term largely depends.

In saying Boutros-Ghali had not done enough to carry out reforms, the Clinton administration faces pressure from its allies and foes alike to pay the outstanding $1.3 billion for dues and peacekeeping to the United Nations.
But so far the Republican-dominated Congress has shown few signs it is willing to pay the arrears quickly.

Many congressmen believe the United States is contributing disproportionately to the United Nations in both dues and voluntary contributions, although most European countries and Japan pay more in relation to their incomes.
Annan, who was the undersecretary-general for peacekeeping operations, is the seventh U.N. secretary-general.
He is also the first from sub-Saharan Africa and the first to have risen through the ranks of the U.N. bureaucracy.

For security reasons he and his wife have been told to move from their flat on Roosevelt Island in the East River to a hotel in Manhattan while the secretary-general's house on elegant Sutton Place was being renovated, U.N. sources said.
